\title{How Close Can a Real-Time Detector Get?\\
Polygon-Encoded YOLO Segmentation for\\
Multi-Structure Echocardiography}

\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Anonymous Submission}
\IEEEauthorblockA{Paper ID \pending{ID}}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Semantic segmentation networks dominate cardiac ultrasound benchmarks, but
their cost is poorly matched to handheld probes. Real-time detectors such as
YOLO are an obvious alternative, yet cannot be applied to the CAMUS label space
directly: the myocardium is an \emph{annulus}, and a YOLO instance mask is a
single polygon, which has no hole. We encode the epicardium as a \emph{filled}
contour and recover the myocardium by subtraction, and quantify what that
representation can express: a perfect model under it reaches $0.997$ Dice at
$0.308$\,mm HD95, exactly one pixel. On the official CAMUS split this yields
$3.809$\,mm HD95 at $2.7$\,M parameters -- the best in the benchmark, ahead of
the strongest baseline by twice the seed noise -- with mean Dice $0.9113$,
statistically indistinguishable from the four leading baselines, and
encoder--decoders scale $4$--$8\times$ with pixel count. The negative result is
the more useful one: having first measured run-to-run variance ($0.134$\,mm
across seeds, which a paired test over 200 frames calls significant), we find
that \emph{no} configuration change we tried improves on the stock setting.
Code and the full experiment plan are released.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
Echocardiography, cardiac segmentation, YOLO, instance segmentation,
real-time inference, CAMUS.
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section*{Compliance with Ethical Standards}
Conducted retrospectively on the publicly available CAMUS
dataset~\cite{leclerc2019camus}; ethical approval was not required, as
confirmed by the licence attached to that dataset.
